connection_type: I'm a caregiver, partner, or close community member of someone with this experience
duration: I have been the father of a queer trans kid for 14 years (aware of it for 1) and a  daughter who is Indigneous and Black
disclosure_text: I have worked with marginalized communities for the majority of my adult life. I identify as a queer person and as someone with a disability, but I also feel that I carry tremendous privilege regardless of these factors. I feel like I was already invested in these topics as a youth, which led me to pursue education in global stewardship, human rights and law. I went on to work with marginalized communities in a legal setting, and working with non profits working on houselessness, government child apprehension and workplace sexual violence. We adopted my daughter who is Inuk, and her family is from Nunavut and try to be aware of how racism and being part of a mixed race family impacts her. My kid came out as queer and later as trans to us just over a year ago and we are navigating how to keep em safe and happy in a world that often challenges eir right to those things.
micronarrative: I connect with the group holding “No one is illegal” signs, finding their energy nurturing and protective, while I don’t understand the violent, hateful energy of the opposing side. I don’t have personal experience with immigration or xenophobia, but I believe I have a better understanding of global issues and human rights crises than those demanding strict border enforcement. This perspective shifted in 2008 when I attended monologues presented by a friend in Vancouver. The university culture there was key, as I saw the juxtaposition of extreme wealth and extreme poverty for the first time, resonating with an overarching narrative of unfairness. I was mostly friends with others from my program, but later I adapted my behavior for family or old friends who hadn’t learned the same things. I was young and headstrong; keeping the peace was the least of my concerns because I thought I was right and didn’t care about much else.

chat_log.content: Reading through that passage — what stands out to you first? Is there something you connect with on a personal level, or something that feels distant?

I think it stands out to me that one group is being violent and hateful with their energy and the other seems to be nurturing and protective. I certainly connect with the group that says no one is illegal and I don't understand the perspective of the other group.
When you say you "certainly connect" with the group holding the "No one is illegal" signs, what specific part of your own background or identity makes that stance feel like home to you?

I have close friends that have participated in work with the no one is illegal campaign. I attended a series of monologues presented by a friend (whose wedding I'm attending in a few weeks) in 2008 which really helped shift my perspective on immigrant and refugee issues. I don't have personal experience with immigration or facing xenophobia personally but I think I have a better understanding of global issues and human rights crises than the folks demanding strict border enforcement.
Where were you living in 2008 when you attended those monologues, and how did the local culture there shape the way those stories were received?

I was living in Vancouver. I think the culture of my program at university was very key to this. I also feel that I was seeing the juxtaposition of extreme wealth and extreme poverty and suffering for the first time. I think the stories I heard resonated with an overarching narrative of unfairness.
In that university environment, did you find yourself shifting your language or tone when moving between academic discussions and other social settings?

Not especially as I was mostly friends with other folks from my program. I would say later on I felt like I was adapting my behaviour depending on who I was dealing with in terms of family or old friends who hadn't learned the same things as me
When you adapted your behavior for those family or old friends, did you find yourself simplifying your language or avoiding certain topics to keep the peace?
Probably not as much as I should have, I was young and headstrong and keeping the peace was the least of my concerns. I thought I was right and didn't care about much else.
What specific memory from that time stands out where your headstrong stance caused a tangible friction with those family or friends?
